text.p: It may seem perverse, but even though the British economy is showing clear signs of overheating, some economists fear it could easily slide into recession.

Gross domestic product (GDP) grew a robust 3.4 percent year-on-year in the second quarter -- the 21st successive quarter of economic growth -- consumer spending is soaring, money supply growth is sky-high and inflation edged higher last month.

This combination would seem to merit a judicious tightening of monetary policy to dampen consumption and indeed, official interest rates have been raised three times in as many months to 6.75 percent.

However, some economists fear higher interest rates, an exceptionally strong pound which is already hurting exporters and tight fiscal policy could jolt Britain into an abrupt "hard landing" next year.

The National Institute of Economic and Social Research (NIESR) sees worrying parallels between the early years of Conservative Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher's first administration, which came to power in 1979, and the conditions which Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair inherited this year.

Stiff increases in interest rates and taxes under Thatcher and a strong currency combined to push the economy into recession in the early 1980s. "If sterling continues to rise in the way it did in 1979 and 1980, then there is a much more significant risk that the early years of the Blair revolution, like the Thatcher revolution, will be marked by a recession," the NIESR said in a report this week.
A recession is generally defined as two successive quarters of negative growth.
Goldman Sachs chief economist Gavyn Davies told parliament's Treasury Select committee this week that the Bank of England already "risked overkill" on rates.

But there is an alternative route to recession. Whereas Davies thinks the economy has already been restrained enough, Bill Martin of UBS sees it accelerating out of control, and heading for bust via a 1980s-style boom. "We might be into overheating territory already and a recession is inevitable and required," he told the parliamentarians.
The Treasury's latest compilation of independent forecasts shows most economists expect GDP growth to slow to a still-comfortable 2.7 percent in 1998 from a projected 3.4 percent this year.

But David Hillier, an economist at BZW, said he is revising down his forecasts for 1998. "Growth in the service sector could fall back to its long-term trend rate while manufacturing could experience a recession," he said. "GDP growth in late 1998 could be closer to 1.5 percent than 2.5 percent."
The new Labour government is determined to break the "boom-bust" economic cycles that have bedevilled Britain for decades.

It has effectively delegated the task of steering the economy through what could prove a critical turning-point to the Bank of England, putting a new Monetary Policy Committee at the Bank in charge of interest rates.

Finance minister Gordon Brown tightened fiscal policy in his first budget on July 2, but tax increases were aimed squarely at the corporate sector and Brown was accused of doing nothing to discourage consumer spending.

The Bank has acknowledged that it faces a dilemma -- rapid domestic demand growth requires higher interest rates, but higher rates would further strengthen the pound and inflict even more pain on struggling manufacturers.

Nevertheless, it has made clear that it will not let the strong pound stop it from administering the monetary medicine it believes the economy needs if inflation is to remain under control. The expectation in the City of London is that interest rates will go still higher.

However, a "shadow" monetary committee of leading economists, some of whom advised the last Conservative government, told the Bank this week that the three quarter-point interest rate rises of the past three months were enough.
Sir Alan Walters, a former adviser to Thatcher, reminded the committee "of the speed at which the economy deflated in the early 1980s."
There are still many optimists in the City, however.

Simon Briscoe and Edmund Nonis of Nikko Europe say the current "boomlet" in consumer spending should be seen in context. It is not nearly as strong as late 1980s levels, they say, and is largely a result of around 35 billion pounds ($58.5 billion) of "windfall" payments to consumers from the conversion of mutually owned building societies into banks.
The windfalls are a one-off occurrence which will not increase consumer spending power indefinitely.

"Growth will be above trend this year as a result of the building society windfalls, but at around 3-1/4 percent and with the prospect of falling back below 3.0 percent in 1998, there is little to get very worried about," the Nikko economists wrote in their latest economic quarterly.

For David Philpotts, an economist at Schroders, strong consumer confidence and rampant money supply growth awaken memories of the boom of the late 1980s, which was followed by Britain's longest post-war recession.
"The probability of a harder landing in growth is increasing every day sterling remains strong," he says.

But Philpotts believes consumer confidence may ebb once the flow of building society windfalls into consumers' pockets ceases. "We still do not see a recession, at least outside manufacturing," he says. ($ = 0.598 British Pounds)
